title: Redwood Private VPC security architecture deep dive with Cobalt Banking
summary: Deep dive on Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem) security architecture focusing on network isolation, ingress/egress controls, firewalling, encryption/KMS, audit logs and compliance alignment (SOC 2/ISO). Agreed to share SOC2 pack, network diagram, and schedule follow-up bench/PoC for ingress/egress testing.
next_steps: Jordan Lee: Share SOC2 report, current pen test summary, and Redwood private network diagram (due 2027-01-20)
Maya Patel: Prep a checklist for KMS/HSM integration and key rotation options (due 2027-01-22)
Noah Rivers & Samir Kaur: Provide VPC CIDR ranges and approved egress IPs for whitelisting (due 2027-01-19)
Schedule lab PoC for ingress/egress and firewall rules verification (target week of 2027-01-25)
Set follow-up call to review audit log forwarding and SIEM ingest (target 2027-01-27)
action_items: Jordan Lee: Share SOC2 report, pen test summary, and network diagram; due 2027-01-20
Maya Patel: Document KMS/HSM integration options and sample key rotation policy; due 2027-01-22

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-15
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Carlos Gomez (Redwood SE), Evelyn Hart (Cobalt Head of Security), Noah Rivers (Cobalt Cloud Architect), Priya Das (Cobalt Compliance), Samir Kaur (Cobalt Network)

[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Jordan from Redwood here, i'm joined by maya and carlos on the technical side. how's everyone doing?
[00:08] Evelyn Hart: Good, thanks. lot to cover, appreciate the deep dive.
[00:12] Noah Rivers: Hi all. we want to focus on VPC/private deployment details 	6 ingress, egress, firewalling, and how KMS/HSM and audit logs integrate with our SIEM.
[00:20] Maya Patel: Great 	6 we'll walk through the architecture we recommend for Redwood Private in a VPC, call out isolation patterns, and then discuss controls for compliance 	6 SOC 2 / ISO. sound good?
[00:27] Priya Das: Yes, and we need to validate log retention, who has access, and data residency guarantees.
[00:34] Jordan Lee: Quick note 	6 we shared a one-pager earlier but this will get into network flow. also apologies if auto transcript misnames things, sometimes redwoods comes out as redwood's etc.

[00:45] Carlos Gomez: Ok first slide 	6 high level: Redwood Private runs a control plane that can be hosted by us or deployed as a customer-managed control plane; compute nodes (inference runtime) live in your VPC subnets. common pattern is private subnets for worker nodes, a management subnet for control-plane egress, and a bastion/admin subnet for ops access.
[01:05] Samir Kaur: so the inference nodes never have public IPs?
[01:09] Maya Patel: Correct 	6 no public IPs on worker instances. inbound traffic is via an ingress gateway or load balancer that you control in a DMZ subnet or via private link. we support both options 	6 ALB/NLB with internal addresses, or AWS PrivateLink style endpoints.
[01:24] Evelyn Hart: For our auditors, we need to show that there's no direct internet ingress to workloads and every egress is controlled. how do you handle outbound updates/telemetry?
[01:33] Carlos Gomez: Outbound egress uses NAT or managed egress proxies. we give you a list of Redwood egress IP ranges that you can allowlist, or we can configure traffic to go through your egress firewall/proxy. telemetry and metrics can be forwarded to your logging stack 	6 we don't send raw customer data to our hosted telemetry by default in private mode.
[01:48] Noah Rivers: If we want to force all egress through our network firewall for inspection, is there a supported pattern?
[01:53] Maya Patel: Yes 	6 use route table entries to direct nat gateway/egress through your inspection appliance. or run a dedicated NAT twin per AZ pointing to your firewall cluster. Redwood's runtime initiates all outbound connections, so as long as your egress devices allow the outbound to our known endpoints the flows work.
[02:10] Evelyn Hart: And what about TLS termination 	6 where are certificates terminated? we can't have plaintext egress.
[02:15] Carlos Gomez: TLS stays end-to-end. inference clients connect over mTLS or TLS to the ingress endpoint. For control plane (if customer-managed) the control plane components also use mTLS with mutual auth. we integrate with your ACM or KMS for certs, or you can upload your own.

[02:30] Samir Kaur: Firewalling 	6 we run strict deny-by-default at perimeter. can you provide recommended security groups and NACL rules?
[02:36] Maya Patel: Absolutely 	6 we provide a hardened baseline: worker security groups locked to the control-plane on specific ports (gRPC 443 and a management port 8443 for admin), allow only internal subnet ranges, and NACL suggested ephemeral port ranges. we'll share a ruleset.
[02:50] Priya Das: For SOC 2, auditors want to see RBAC and SSO 	6 how is admin access handled?
[02:55] Jordan Lee: We support SAML 2.0/SO single sign-on via your identity provider. RBAC is role-based in the console with integration to your SAML groups, and you can map to least-privilege roles. All admin actions are logged to the audit trail.
[03:10] Evelyn Hart: Do audit logs leave our VPC? we prefer logs forwarded to our SIEM and stored on-prem for retention.
[03:17] Carlos Gomez: We can forward logs to your Logstash/CloudWatch/ELK via private endpoints. By default logs can be written to a customer-managed S3 bucket or object store inside your VPC, and we can push events to your SIEM via a Firehose or syslog aggregator. nothing needs to go to Redwood-managed storage unless you opt-in.
[03:34] Noah Rivers: Good. what's the retention policy in Redwood if we asked you to keep logs for the pilot?
[03:38] Maya Patel: For private deployments we typically recommend customer-managed retention. If Redwood stores anything (for operational troubleshooting) it's configurable 	6 default 30 days but we can adjust and provide encryption at rest. We'll also provide log redaction options for PII.

[03:55] Jordan Lee: On encryption/KMS 	6 we support using your KMS or cloud HSM for at-rest keys. you can choose customer-managed keys (CMKs) in AWS KMS or on-prem HSM integrations. keys are only in your KMS, Redwood never has access to plaintext keys.
[04:10] Evelyn Hart: So you support BYOK 	6 bring-your-own-key?
[04:13] Maya Patel: Yes, BYOK for model artifacts and state. For ephemeral caches like KV cache in-memory it's encrypted in memory, and persisted checkpoints are encrypted with CMK. For model weights if stored on object storage we use SSE-KMS with your key.
[04:27] Priya Das: We need key rotation policies that meet our SOC2 control matrix. can you show rotation cadence and rotation without downtime?
[04:33] Carlos Gomez: We support key rotation via KMS key aliases 	6 you rotate keys within your KMS and then update the alias binding, Redwood will pick up the new alias automatically. for long-lived artifacts we re-encrypt on next write; there may be a short coordinated window for bulk re-encrypt if you require immediate rotation. we'll document a recommended rotation cadence 	6 90 days is typical for keys used in higher-sensitivity contexts, but depends on your policy.

[04:55] Noah Rivers: Who holds the root of trust for keys? if we use HSM do you ever hold backups?
[04:59] Maya Patel: If you deploy with customer-managed HSM/KMS, Redwood holds no key material. backups of keystores are under your control. if you ask us to provision KMS we can manage keys but for enterprise customers we recommend your KMS/HSM.

[05:12] Samir Kaur: Network isolation question 	6 can we put inference nodes in multiple isolated subnets and only allow the inference API to be in a single DMZ? we want minimal attack surface.
[05:20] Carlos Gomez: Yes 	6 a common pattern is put the ingress gateway in a narrow DMZ/ingress subnet and then have worker pools in private subnets with no inbound. The ingress then forwards to internal load balancers on private IPs. Worker nodes talk to control plane over mTLS and use security group allowances.
[05:36] Evelyn Hart: For regulators, data residency is critical 	6 our customer data must not leave EU region. can Redwood guarantee that?
[05:43] Jordan Lee: In private mode, you can deploy entirely in your region 	6 control plane and compute inside your VPC in eu-west-1, for example. Redwood will provide a deployment config that pins everything to that region. No cross-region replication unless explicitly configured.
[05:57] Priya Das: We'll need language in the contract for that 	6 can you add region-only processing commitments?
[06:02] Jordan Lee: Yes, we can add data residency clauses and include them in the SOW for private deployments. We'll surface baseline contract language for legal review.

[06:15] Noah Rivers: Let's talk ingress options 	6 private link vs internal load balancer vs VPN. pros/cons?
[06:21] Maya Patel: PrivateLink gives you a single-tenant endpoint with no public IP space and avoids NAT complexities. Internal LB works well with ALB/NLB, simpler if you already use internal LBs. VPN can be used for on-prem connectivity or for management. If you want deep inspection at perimeter, put an internal LB in front of inspection appliances. PrivateLink reduces attack surface and is often preferred by banks.
[06:40] Samir Kaur: For PrivateLink, do we need to accept peering requests or do you create the endpoint?
[06:45] Carlos Gomez: The customer creates the interface endpoint and accepts the service in their account. we provide the service name. we'll walk through the steps in the runbook.

[06:55] Evelyn Hart: IDS/IPS 	6 do you have recommendations? we run a managed detection stack and prefer to forward flow logs to them.
[07:01] Maya Patel: Send VPC flow logs and ALB logs to your SIEM. we can also export application-level audit logs. For host-level detection you can run an agent on worker images; we support common EDR agents in hardened mode.
[07:13] Priya Das: About auditability 	6 can we get tamper-evident logs?
[07:16] Carlos Gomez: We can sign event batches and put append-only logs into your S3 with object lock or into a WORM store to meet tamper-evidence requirements. We'll include sample configs.

[07:30] Jordan Lee: Switching gear 	6 now firewalling specifics. most customers use deny-all then open minimal ports. we recommend restricting management ports to your admin CIDR and use a bastion with MFA.
[07:42] Samir Kaur: MFA for bastion? we prefer hardware keys.
[07:44] Maya Patel: Supported 	6 we integrate with SAML providers that can enforce hardware MFA or Yubikey flows. bastion access ideally via ephemeral certificates and session recording.
[07:56] Noah Rivers: Are there any agent footprint concerns? we run a hardened image set.
[08:00] Carlos Gomez: Our runtime is containerized; we provide hardened images with a small agent for telemetry. If you want no agents, we can do a sidecarless setup but you lose some observability 	6 we can route metrics via sidecar proxies that you manage.

[08:18] Evelyn Hart: On compliance mapping 	6 do you have a SOC 2 Type II report and an ISO 27001 cert?
[08:23] Jordan Lee: Yes 	6 we have SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 for our hosted control plane and we provide a SOC2 bridge letter and scope doc for private customers. we'll share redacted reports and an architecture scope showing which controls are in customer scope versus vendor scope.
[08:40] Priya Das: We'll need the control matrix mapping for our auditor 	6 show who is responsible for each control.
[08:44] Maya Patel: We'll share a RACI-style matrix aligning Redwood controls and customer controls. often network controls remain customer responsibility but we provide runbooks and hardened defaults.

[08:58] Noah Rivers: Something practical 	6 we need a list of ports/IPs and a sample firewall ruleset we can hand to our firewall team.
[09:04] Carlos Gomez: We'll attach a recommended ruleset: inbound to ingress LB: 443 mTLS, health-check port 8080 from ALB, internal gRPC 443 between services, management 8443 only from admin CIDR. outbound allowlist for Redwood endpoints on 443 and optionally 443 for telemetry; ephemeral ranges for node management.
[09:24] Samir Kaur: Do you publish a stable set of egress IPs? our firewall team hates rotating IP ranges.
[09:29] Maya Patel: We publish egress IP ranges for dedicated pools; for private we can provide static IPs via NAT gateway Elastic IPs or endpoints so they stay stable. we'll document them in the SOW.

[09:42] Evelyn Hart: Encryption in transit 	6 you mentioned mTLS. Can we require mutual TLS for all inter-service traffic including control plane?
[09:49] Carlos Gomez: Yes 	6 mutual TLS for control plane and customer traffic is supported. certs can be managed by your identity infra; we also provide automatic cert rotation for service certs if you prefer.

[09:58] Priya Das: For legal, we need assurance on vulnerability management and patch windows. what's your SLAs?
[10:03] Jordan Lee: For private deployments we follow a scheduled maintenance cadence; critical patches are accelerated. we provide CVE summaries and patch dates in the security pack. For Dedicated customers we can agree on maintenance windows and notifications.

[10:18] Noah Rivers: Could you describe the incident response path? who do we call and how are incidents escalated?
[10:22] Maya Patel: We'll be your escalation path for Redwood-managed components. we provide a 24/7 pager for Sev1 incidents as an add-on, plus a runbook that includes contact points, expected RTOs and how we collaborate with your IR team.

[10:35] Jordan Lee: Let's do a quick demo of a sample network diagram. (screen share) so here's the DMZ ingress, internal ALB, worker subnets per AZ, NAT in each AZ forwarding to your firewall cluster, S3 for logs with server-side encryption using your CMK, and PrivateLink endpoints for control-plane API access.
[10:58] Samir Kaur: Looks good. can you show the flow for a model update from your image registry to the worker nodes? we need to ensure signed images and integrity checks.
[11:05] Carlos Gomez: Model artifacts are signed; we support image signing (cosign) and artifacts come with sha256 digests. the deployment pipeline verifies signatures against a trust root. we can integrate with your image registry immutability and scanning tools.
[11:20] Evelyn Hart: For proof to auditors, can we run a small PoC where you show logs flowing to our SIEM and we validate firewall rules?
[11:26] Jordan Lee: Absolutely 	6 that's the plan. we'll run a 2-week lab PoC scoped to ingress/egress and log forwarding.

[11:35] Priya Das: A couple of nitty-gritty Qs: Do you support VPC endpoint policies to restrict S3 writes to only specific prefixes?
[11:40] Maya Patel: Yes 	6 you can use VPC endpoint policies, bucket policies, and IAM conditions to restrict writes to specific prefixes. We recommend combining IAM, bucket policies, and S3 Object Lock for tamper evidence.

[11:52] Noah Rivers: Can Redwood rotate instance credentials automatically or do we manage that?
[11:56] Carlos Gomez: We can integrate with your secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager or HashiCorp Vault). Redwood can request short-lived credentials and we support IAM roles for service accounts to avoid long-lived secrets.

[12:08] Samir Kaur: Any recommended network monitoring for TLS inspection? we suspect we will want to decrypt some flows for advanced inspection.
[12:14] Maya Patel: If you need TLS inspection, you can terminate TLS at your inspection cluster in the DMZ and then re-encrypt to internal endpoints. Be aware that mTLS between services would need to be re-established 	6 we can support certificate re-issuance via your CA for internal services.

[12:29] Jordan Lee: Ok, wrapping up with compliance specifics. we'll share the SOC2 Type II and ISO scope, the RACI matrix, recommended firewall ruleset, and a runbook for PrivateLink setup.
[12:40] Evelyn Hart: We'll review and feed back. legal will want the residency clause and specific audit rights.
[12:45] Priya Das: Also please include an example of the audit log schema and sample events so our SIEM team can map fields.
[12:52] Carlos Gomez: Will do 	6 sample events plus field mappings.

[13:00] Jordan Lee: Final recap of next steps: Jordan to send SOC2 + network diagram; Maya to send KMS/HSM checklist; we'll schedule PoC for week of 2027-01-25; Noah and Samir to provide VPC ranges. Any objections?
[13:12] Noah Rivers: No objections, sounds good.
[13:15] Evelyn Hart: Thanks, appreciate the detail.
[13:18] Priya Das: Thanks everyone.
[13:20] Jordan Lee: Thanks all 	6 we'll follow up with notes and the security pack.

End transcript.

Notes on transcription: speaker labels occasionally merged, some technical terms (KV cache) transcribed as K V cash, and product names may appear as redwoods in a few spots. The technical content above reflects the intended conversation and action items agreed upon.
